_source: Documented herb-drug interaction pairs from: Natural Medicines Comprehensive Database, WHO Herbal Safety Monographs, Stargrove et al. 'Herb, Nutrient, and Drug Interactions' (2008), Memorial Sloan Kettering About Herbs database, and Cochrane systematic reviews.
_note: herbName and drugName are lowercase normalized. drugName may refer to a specific drug or a class. Multiple entries per herb cover different drug classes.

interactions.description: Curcumin (the active compound in turmeric) inhibits platelet aggregation and has mild anticoagulant activity. Combined use with warfarin may potentiate anticoagulation, increasing bleeding risk. INR monitoring is advised if concurrent use cannot be avoided. Sources: Natural Medicines Database, multiple case reports.

Turmeric/curcumin inhibits thromboxane synthesis and platelet aggregation through similar but additive pathways to aspirin. Combined use can increase bleeding risk, particularly in patients with gastrointestinal vulnerabilities or on dual antiplatelet therapy.

Curcumin has demonstrated antiplatelet activity via inhibition of arachidonic acid metabolism. Concurrent use with clopidogrel may additively inhibit platelet function, raising the risk of bruising, prolonged bleeding, or haemorrhage.

Turmeric has demonstrated modest blood pressure-lowering effects in clinical studies. Combined use with antihypertensive drugs (ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, ARBs) may produce additive hypotension, particularly in higher-dose supplementation.

Curcumin is the bioactive constituent of turmeric. It inhibits platelet aggregation and coagulation cascade enzymes. Combined use with warfarin is associated with raised INR and increased bleeding risk in published case reports.

Ginger (Zingiber officinale) contains gingerols and shogaols that inhibit thromboxane synthetase and platelet aggregation. Combined use with warfarin has been associated with raised INR and spontaneous bruising in case reports. Monitor INR closely.

Ginger has antiplatelet properties that may be additive with aspirin's COX-1 inhibition. Combined use at high ginger supplement doses may mildly increase bleeding time. Most relevant in post-operative patients or those with gastric mucosal fragility.

Clinical studies have shown ginger can modestly reduce fasting blood glucose. Combined use with antidiabetic drugs (metformin, sulfonylureas, insulin) may have additive hypoglycaemic effects, increasing the risk of low blood sugar.

Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) has documented anxiolytic and mild CNS depressant properties (GABA-A receptor modulation). Combined use with benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, or sedating antihistamines may produce additive central nervous system depression, drowsiness, and psychomotor impairment.

Ashwagandha has been shown in clinical trials to stimulate thyroid hormone synthesis (T3/T4 elevation). Combined use with levothyroxine or thyroid replacement therapy may produce thyrotoxic effects (palpitations, anxiety, weight loss). Thyroid function should be monitored.

Ashwagandha has demonstrated immunostimulatory activity (NK cell activation, macrophage stimulation). This may antagonize the therapeutic effect of immunosuppressive drugs used post-transplant or in autoimmune conditions (tacrolimus, cyclosporine, corticosteroids).

Garlic supplements contain allicin which inhibits platelet aggregation and fibrinolysis. Multiple case reports and pharmacological studies document warfarin potentiation with garlic supplementation, resulting in elevated INR and bleeding episodes. Documented in Natural Medicines Database.

High-dose garlic supplements significantly induce CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, leading to markedly reduced plasma concentrations of HIV antiretroviral drugs (saquinavir reduced by ~50% in pharmacokinetic studies). This may lead to therapeutic failure and viral resistance.

Ginkgo biloba inhibits platelet-activating factor (PAF) and has direct antiplatelet activity. Combined with warfarin, it can significantly increase bleeding risk. Multiple case reports of spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage in patients on concurrent warfarin and ginkgo. High-severity interaction.

Ginkgo biloba's PAF-inhibiting antiplatelet effects combined with aspirin's COX-1 inhibition produce additive antiplatelet activity. This combination has been associated with spontaneous haemorrhage in published case reports.

Ginkgo biloba may lower seizure threshold and reduce the efficacy of antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine), possibly through induction of drug-metabolising enzymes. Case reports of seizure recurrence in controlled epilepsy exist.
Valeriana officinalis enhances GABAergic transmission. Combined use with benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or sedatives causes excessive daytime sedation and respiratory depression.

Valerian may have pharmacodynamic synergy with alprazolam (Xanax) and other benzodiazepines via GABA-A receptor modulation. This may potentiate sedation, memory impairment, and psychomotor depression. Avoid concurrent use without clinical supervision.

Echinacea is an immunostimulant and may counteract the therapeutic intent of immunosuppressive drugs (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, azathioprine) used in transplant patients or autoimmune disease. Risk of graft rejection or disease flare with concurrent use.

Echinacea preparations have been rarely associated with hepatotoxicity. Combined use with other hepatotoxic drugs (statins, isoniazid, methotrexate) may increase liver enzyme elevation risk. Liver function monitoring is recommended in long-term use.
Panax ginseng has been shown to reduce blood levels of warfarin and decrease INR response. Frequent INR surveillance recommended.
Ginseng enhances insulin sensitivity and pancreatic beta-cell function. Concomitant use with insulin or sulfonylureas increases the likelihood of hypoglycemia.
Licorice-induced sodium and water retention elevates systemic vascular resistance, neutralizing blood pressure control from antihypertensive medications.
Licorice-induced hypokalemia profoundly sensitizes cardiac myocytes to digoxin toxicity, triggering fatal arrhythmias and heart block.

Hypericum perforatum inhibits reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. Combined use with SSRIs, SNRIs, or TCAs significantly increases the risk of severe Serotonin Syndrome (hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rigidity).

St. John's Wort is a potent inducer of hepatic CYP3A4 enzymes and intestinal P-glycoprotein. It accelerates estrogen and progestin clearance, resulting in breakthrough bleeding and unintended pregnancy.
Induces CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, substantially reducing plasma warfarin concentrations, causing sudden drop in INR and heightened risk of thromboembolism.
P-glycoprotein induction decreases digoxin bioavailability by up to 25-40%, precipitating loss of heart rate and cardiac rhythm control in heart failure/atrial fibrillation.
Massive induction of CYP3A4 clearance reduces immunosuppressive drug levels, directly documented to cause acute organ transplant rejection.
Green tea extracts contain substantial amounts of Vitamin K, directly antagonizing the anticoagulant action of warfarin and lowering therapeutic INR.

Epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG) inhibits organic anion-transporting polypeptide (OATP1A2/OATP1B1), significantly decreasing the intestinal absorption and bioavailability of beta-blockers like nadolol and atenolol.
EGCG modulates hepatic OATP transport and CYP3A4 metabolism, altering plasma concentrations of atorvastatin and simvastatin.
Coenzyme Q10 shares chemical structural homology with Vitamin K (menaquinone). It can diminish warfarin's anticoagulant efficacy, causing sub-therapeutic INR and clot risk.
CoQ10 has mild intrinsic vasodilatory and blood pressure-lowering properties. Concomitant use with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or CCBs can cause additive hypotension.

Melatonin combined with benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam) or Z-drugs (zolpidem) results in profound central nervous system depression, impaired psychomotor performance, and increased risk of nocturnal falls.
Exogenous melatonin may impair nocturnal blood pressure dip and has been reported to interfere with the efficacy of calcium channel blockers (nifedipine).

Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum / Methi) seeds contain 4-hydroxyisoleucine and galactomannan which stimulate insulin release and delay glucose absorption, causing additive hypoglycemia with metformin and sulfonylureas.
Fenugreek contains natural coumarin derivatives. Co-administration with warfarin or antiplatelet agents increases the risk of bleeding.
Holy Basil (Ocimum sanctum / Tulsi) exhibits antiplatelet and anticoagulant properties via cyclooxygenase inhibition, synergistically increasing bleeding risks with warfarin, aspirin, or clopidogrel.
Tulsi has documented hypoglycemic action. When combined with oral antidiabetics (metformin, glimepiride), monitor for sudden blood glucose drops.

Glycyrrhizin in licorice inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, inducing apparent mineralocorticoid excess (pseudoaldosteronism) causing severe hypokalemia, sodium retention, and ventricular arrhythmia with loop diuretics (furosemide).

Piper methysticum (Kava) is strongly hepatotoxic and depletes hepatic glutathione reserves. Concurrent use with paracetamol (acetaminophen) significantly accelerates hepatic injury and acute liver failure risk.
Ginkgolide B is a potent platelet-activating factor (PAF) antagonist. When co-administered with NSAIDs like ibuprofen, multiple clinical reports document spontaneous hyphema and subdural hematomas.
